# Findings — Hebrew typing, measured

*Written for a reader who does not work on this project. Every number here is regenerated by
`scripts/reproduce.sh` from committed inputs. Nothing below is a summary of a result you cannot
re-run.*

---

## The rule everything here was produced under

**A gate that has never failed has not been shown to be a gate.** Every check in this repository
runs a **planted defect first** and reports `NOT-A-GATE` if the planted defect comes back green.
Every experiment commits its predictions and its stopping rule **before** the harness exists,
and every bar is measured against a baseline **re-measured in the same run** rather than against
a published constant.

The discipline is not decoration. **It corrected four numbers this project had already
published**, and most experiments run under it ended NOT ADOPTED.

---

## 1. The Hebrew bracket fix that ships to billions of phones makes every measured axis worse

Android's AOSP keyboard defines, for Hebrew:

    keyspec_left_parenthesis  = "(|)"
    keyspec_right_parenthesis = ")|("

`KeySpecParser`'s own javadoc documents that format as `keyLabel|keyOutputText`. **So the key
labelled `(` commits U+0029.** That is not a rendering trick — it changes the character in the
user's text. FUTO Keyboard's fork carries the same values, and its one Hebrew release note reads
*"Fixed some behavior when it comes to typing parentheses in Hebrew"* (v0.1.27, 2024-12-25).

Measured against **3,257 lines of Hebrew a person actually typed**:

| | bracket lines that render differently between apps | fixes | breaks | text survives copy-paste |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| commit what the label says | 355 of 463 (**77%**) | — | — | — |
| **swap the character — what AOSP ships** | 399 of 463 (**86%**) | **0 of 952** | **60** | **no** |
| two invisible direction marks | **0 of 463 (0%)** | 641 of 952 | **0** | yes |

Bracket divergence rises from 77% to 86%. It repairs nothing, breaks sixty lines that were
stable, and it is the only approach measured here that alters a character rather than adding a
format control — so text copied out of the field is not the text the user meant, and a search
for it will not match.

**A hypothesis this supports, labelled as one:** the complaint Hebrew users file against these
keyboards — *"הסוגריים תמיד יוצאים הפוכים"*, quoted at two stars — may be **caused by the fix
rather than by its absence.** Swapping the committed character makes bracketed Hebrew look right
inside a Hebrew-locale app and wrong everywhere else.

**And it is not a claim that anyone was careless.** The swap was correct for the case that was
overwhelmingly common when it was written: a Hebrew app, Hebrew paragraph direction. What
changed is that people now type Hebrew into apps whose locale is English, and a fix that lives
in the committed character cannot travel.

**Not measured:** Gboard is closed source. It descends from the same codebase and may differ.
The oracle is `java.text.Bidi`, the algorithm — not Android's `TextView`.

---

## 2. Transcribed Hebrew and typed Hebrew do not share an alphabet

Every Hebrew NLP benchmark built on transcription or encyclopedia text is blind to characters
typists produce constantly. Share of lines containing at least one such character:

| | transcribed (OpenSubtitles, 3,000,000 lines) | typed (Ynet comments, MIT) | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| **geresh / gershayim** — the marks inside every Hebrew abbreviation | **0.01%** | **3.57%** | **×604** |
| **brackets** | **0.21%** | **5.71%** | **×27** |
| emoji | 0.00% | 1.27% | ×458 |
| a Latin letter | 0.52% | 2.91% | ×6 |

**Why this is not a curiosity.** This project's own evaluation corpora keep only `[א-ת]+` runs.
That one filter deleted every character above, was never registered as a decision, and no check
noticed for four milestones. It made a bracket experiment on those corpora return **exactly zero
divergence on 12,000 lines** — a corpus without brackets cannot show a bracket problem.

**Not measured:** neither register is phone messaging. Facebook comments are typed, which is the
axis under test, and they are still not messages.

---

## 3. Register is worth a factor of 2.3 to word prediction and almost nothing to spelling correction

The same shipped code, the same configuration, three registers measured in one run:

| | encyclopedic | transcribed | **typed** |
|---|---|---|---|
| completion from one letter, top-3 | 5.43% | **23.72%** | **10.33%** [9.75, 10.92] |
| spelling correction, top-1 | 52.60% | — | **51.15%** |

**This project had published *"on the register a phone keyboard is actually used in… 23.72%"*.**
Transcribed dialogue is not that register — it is speech, written down by a professional. On the
closest register a person typed, the same code scores **10.33%**. The direction survives; the
magnitude was overstated by a factor of **2.3**, and the honest sentence is *better than one
suggestion in ten*, not one in four.

**Correction barely moved: 1.45 points.** The asymmetry has a visible mechanism. Correction is a
local edit-distance search over a dictionary, and the dictionary covers both registers about
equally — 99.16% of conversational tokens are present as surface forms against 95.01% of
encyclopedic ones. Prediction depends on a bigram model, which carries the register of whatever
corpus built it.

**The practical reading: a Hebrew keyboard's dictionary generalises across registers and its
prediction model does not.**

---

## 4. A feature was withdrawn because it was right one time in six

The layer that catches a correctly-spelled word in the wrong place — `אם` where `עם` was meant —
was measured against a Hebrew speaker's **blind judgement on 320 real firings**. Precision is
bounded at **[12.5%, 39.7%]**, against a rule registered *before* those labels existed that calls
anything under 40% withdrawable. **The ceiling does not reach the floor of the rule**, and
margin, letter-pair and frequency restrictions were each swept without rescuing it.

**4.83 false alarms per true positive.** A suggestion strip that is wrong five times in six
teaches a user to stop reading the strip — including when it is right about something else. The
harm is not contained to the layer causing it.

It was withdrawn rather than waived. Renegotiating a pre-registered rule once the data arrives is
the thing pre-registration exists to prevent.

---

## What this work does not establish

**Nothing here was measured on a phone, and nothing was measured on a person.** No latency
figure, no user. Of the open questions this project tracks, **37 of 78 need a device or a
human**, and no amount of further work on a build host closes one of them.

Every claim above is a claim about an algorithm or a corpus. None is a claim about how any
keyboard feels to use.

---

## Reproducing this

    TYPED_DIR=<clone>/data HEWIKI_TITLES=<path> ./scripts/reproduce.sh

Each block prints its own positive control before its numbers. **If a control comes back green,
the numbers under it are void** — the harness says so rather than leaving it to the reader.

Corpora: OPUS OpenSubtitles v2018 Hebrew (streamed, never stored); Amram et al. 2018 Ynet
comments (MIT); Hebrew Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0); Wikidata Lexemes (CC0). Full provenance with
hashes in `docs/CORPUS_REGISTER.md`.
